article.Citation: Alper KR, Lotsof HS, Frenken GMN, Luciano DJ, Bastiaans J. Treatment of Acute Opioid Withdrawal with Ibogaine. The American Journal on Addictions. 1999.
article.Title: Treatment of Acute Opioid Withdrawal with Ibogaine

ae_events.Description: Sweating at 24h in one patient, resolved by 48h; also present in a separate treatment-failure case with persistent withdrawal signs.
Chills present at 24 and 48h in one abstinent patient; also occurred in a separate treatment-failure case with persistent withdrawal.
Nausea reported in the treatment-failure case and in the fatal case ~17h post-ibogaine, ~2h before respiratory arrest; no intervention documented.
Muscle aches reported in the treatment-failure case and in the fatal case at 17h post-ibogaine; no intervention documented.
Dilated pupils (mydriasis) observed in the treatment-failure case as part of persistent objective opioid-withdrawal signs post-ibogaine.
Respiratory arrest ~18h post-ibogaine (29 mg/kg) in a 24-year-old female; pronounced dead ~19h post-treatment; cause of death undetermined.

article.PosResult: Authors report 25/33 (76%) fully resolved opioid withdrawal without drug seeking through 72 hours and conclude the series 'appears to provide some evidence for the efficacy of ibogaine in acute opioid withdrawal,' indicating a positive result on the study's own primary outcome despite one fatality and a few non-responders/relapsers.
article.IsObservational: Retrospective case series of 33 patients drawn from an existing informal, non-medical ibogaine treatment network, selected from 41 cases reviewed at a 1995 NIDA meeting; 'open label' here describes uncontrolled real-world delivery observed as-treated, not a randomized or controlled experimental research protocol, so coded observational (Y).
article.ArmScope: Single-arm case series; all 33 patients received ibogaine with no comparator arm, so N, AE counts, and demographics are inherently scoped to the psychedelic (ibogaine) arm.
article.N: Table 2 explicitly gives N=33 as the analyzed/reported cohort (after excluding 8 of the original 41 NIDA-meeting cases for non-opioid-dependence or missing post-treatment observation); used 33, not 41.
article.PctBIPOC: Table 1 ethnicity reports 32 Caucasian, 1 Surinamese. Treated the single Surinamese-labeled patient as the non-Caucasian/BIPOC case (contrasted explicitly against 'Caucasian' in the same table) => 1/33 = 3.0%.
article.PctIndigenous: Ethnicity was reported only as a Caucasian vs. Surinamese split; no indigenous-specific subgroup was reported, so coded not-reported ('.').
article.NumDistinctAEs: Counted as distinct AE types: sweating, chills, nausea, muscle aches, mydriasis, and fatal respiratory arrest. The first five are framed by the authors mainly as persistence/incomplete resolution of opioid withdrawal signs (treatment failure) rather than novel drug-caused effects, but per the safety-dataset directive to avoid understating harm they were coded as AEs since they are adverse physical signs/symptoms documented in specific patients following ibogaine administration. Excluded the Introduction's general description of the acute ibogaine psychoactive state (panoramic recall, hallucinations, and insomnia 'responsive to sleep medication' with citation to ref. 26) because that passage describes ibogaine treatment generally via prior literature, not a finding specifically reported for this cohort of 33 patients in Results/Table 2.
article.NParticipantsWithAE: Counted 4 distinct patients with >=1 AE: the isolated-sweating patient, the isolated-chills patient, the 27-year-old female treatment-failure case (nausea, chills, muscle aches, sweating, mydriasis), and the fatal case (nausea, muscle aches, respiratory arrest).

ae_events.Alper 1999_AE01: Mild: transient, self-resolved by 48h, no intervention documented; occurrence in the treatment-failure case added no further severity signal.
ae_events.Alper 1999_AE02: Mild: persisted 24-48h but no intervention was documented and the patient remained opioid-abstinent; duration is short of the days-to-weeks functional-impairment threshold for Moderate.
ae_events.Alper 1999_AE03: Mild per rubric (transient symptom, no intervention documented). Note: this symptom occurred ~2h before the fatal respiratory arrest in one patient, but the article does not identify nausea itself as a proximate cause of death, so it was not upgraded to Severe on its own; flagged here for reviewer visibility.
ae_events.Alper 1999_AE04: Mild per rubric, same reasoning as AE03; co-occurred with nausea in both the treatment-failure and fatal cases but is not itself identified as causally linked to the fatal outcome.
ae_events.Alper 1999_AE05: Mild: an expected/commonly-assessed opioid-withdrawal sign (mydriasis) with no intervention documented; patient left the treatment setting after ~8h.
ae_events.Alper 1999_AE06: Severe: death is an FDA seriousness criterion (CTCAE grade 5) regardless of the postmortem causal ambiguity the authors raise (forensic exam reached no definitive cause; possible surreptitious heroin use was suggested by charred tin foil found among the patient's effects). SeveritySource set to 'rubric' because the authors treat this as the central safety concern of the series but do not apply formal CTCAE/SAE terminology. InterventionRequired coded '.' because the article does not describe what, if any, resuscitative measures were attempted between the respiratory arrest and the pronouncement of death at ~19 hours.
